_about: Curated facts for shuttle.html (Space Shuttle Endeavour, OV-105). Every fact carries a source id; see the 'sources' list at the end. Compiled September 2026.

orbiter.name: Endeavour
orbiter.named_for: HMS Endeavour, the Royal Navy ship that carried Captain James Cook on his first voyage of discovery (1768–1771). The name was suggested by one-third of the schools taking part in a national naming competition and chosen by President George H. W. Bush.
orbiter.why_built: Congress approved Endeavour in 1987 to replace Space Shuttle Challenger, lost in 1986. Much of it was built from structural spares made during the construction of Discovery and Atlantis.

milestones.event: Construction contract awarded to Rockwell International
Final landing: STS-134 at Kennedy Space Center
Ferry flight on the Shuttle Carrier Aircraft lands at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX)
"Mission 26": the 12-mile (19 km) road move through Inglewood and Los Angeles begins at 11:30 p.m.
Arrives at the California Science Center at 7:30 p.m.
Opens to the public, displayed horizontally in the Samuel Oschin Pavilion
External Tank ET-94 arrives by barge at Marina del Rey after crossing the Panama Canal
Horizontal display in the Samuel Oschin Pavilion closes
Endeavour hard-mated to ET-94 and the two solid rocket boosters ("Go for Stack")
Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center opens to the public

upgrades.text: A 40-foot (12 m) diameter drag chute that cut landing roll-out from about 3,000 ft (910 m) to 2,000 ft (610 m).
Plumbing and electrical connections for Extended Duration Orbiter (EDO) missions of up to 28 days.

stack.description: The world's only authentic space shuttle system displayed in launch configuration: Endeavour mated to External Tank ET-94 and two solid rocket boosters.

et94.story: ET-94 was built for a Columbia mission. After Columbia was lost in 2003, investigators used many pieces of its foam insulation in tests to understand the accident. It is the last flight-qualified external tank.

go_for_stack.what: Endeavour lifted by a 450-foot crane and mated to the tank

display.status: Stacked vertically inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center; the building opens to the public on November 13, 2026.
features: A 140-foot ascent aboard a gantry-style elevator alongside the stack
A Shuttle Descent Slide that drops 45 feet down a 115-foot-long tube
display.payload_bay_config: Configured as for STS-118, with a pressurized SPACEHAB module in the payload bay; the Canadarm and boom on display are Canadian-owned replicas (Endeavour's flown arm is in Ottawa).

visit.address: 700 Exposition Park Drive, Los Angeles, CA 90037
visit.admission: General admission to the California Science Center is free.
visit.air_space_center: Timed reservations for entry to the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center can be made in advance for a small service fee (opens November 13, 2026).
visit.transit: Two blocks west of the Harbor (110) Freeway at Exposition Boulevard; near the Expo Park/USC Metro station.

nose.title: Nose cap
nose.text: The blunt nose meets the hottest air on re-entry. It is capped with Reinforced Carbon-Carbon (RCC): carbon-fibre cloth in a carbon matrix, coated with silicon carbide against oxidation. The same grey material forms the wing leading edges.

windows.title: Flight deck windows
windows.text: The commander and pilot look out through six forward windshields. Two overhead windows and two aft windows look up and back into the payload bay, used when flying the robot arm and docking. Every window has redundant pressure panes.

tiles.title: Black heat-shield tiles
tiles.text: The belly is covered in black silica tiles — mostly empty space, so heat crosses them very slowly. The black Reaction Cured Glass coating sheds heat by radiation. Each tile was shaped for one exact place on the vehicle.

blankets.title: White thermal blankets
blankets.tag: Felt / Advanced Flexible Reusable Surface Insulation
blankets.text: Upper surfaces heat far less on re-entry. They are covered with quilted Advanced Flexible Reusable Surface Insulation (AFRSI) blankets and Felt Reusable Surface Insulation (FRSI); the white finish also keeps the orbiter cool in direct sunlight in orbit.

wing.title: Double-delta wing
wing.text: Two sweep angles: a steep 81° inner glove for stability at hypersonic speed and a 45° outer panel for lift as a glider. Elevons along the trailing edge act as both elevators and ailerons. The orbiter came home as an unpowered glider.

tail.title: Rudder and speed brake
tail.text: The rudder is split vertically into two halves. Swinging together they steer; flaring apart like a clamshell they become a speed brake for the approach and landing. Endeavour also introduced a 12 m (40 ft) drag chute to shorten roll-out.

oms.title: Orbital Maneuvering System (OMS) pods
oms.text: Two pods beside the tail each hold one AJ10-190 engine plus Reaction Control System (RCS) thrusters. The OMS engines raised and changed the orbit and fired the de-orbit burn that brought the orbiter home.

engines.title: Three RS-25 main engines
engines.text: The main engines burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fed from the External Tank for about eight and a half minutes. After retirement the flight engines were removed and kept for the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket; retired orbiters carry replica nozzles.

bay.title: Payload bay and radiators
bay.text: The bay carried satellites, Spacelab, the Hubble servicing tools and whole space station modules. Radiator panels on the inside of the doors dumped heat, so the doors had to be opened soon after reaching orbit. On display, the bay is set up as on STS-118 with a SPACEHAB module.

arm.title: Canadarm
arm.text: A 15 m robot arm built in Canada by Spar Aerospace, with shoulder, elbow and wrist joints like a human arm. Endeavour's flown arm is on display at the Canada Aviation and Space Museum in Ottawa; the arm in Los Angeles is a Canadian-owned replica.

gear.title: Landing gear
gear.text: Tricycle landing gear stowed behind tiled doors. Endeavour made 18 landings at Kennedy Space Center (KSC) in Florida and 7 at Edwards Air Force Base (EAFB) in California.

et.title: External Tank ET-94
et.text: The orange colour is spray-on foam insulation. ET-94 was built for a Columbia mission; after Columbia was lost in 2003 investigators used pieces of its foam in tests. It crossed the Panama Canal by barge and reached Marina del Rey on 18 May 2016.

srb.title: Solid Rocket Boosters
srb.text: Two reusable boosters gave most of the lift-off thrust, burned for about two minutes, then separated and parachuted into the ocean to be recovered. The pair on display were assembled from segments that flew on various Shuttle missions.

missions.purpose: Rescue and redeploy the INTELSAT VI communications satellite
Spacelab-J, a joint mission with Japan
missions.note: Mae Jemison became the first African-American woman in space.

missions.purpose: Deploy the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite TDRS-F
SPACEHAB module; retrieve the European Retrievable Carrier (EURECA)
First Hubble Space Telescope servicing mission
missions.note: Astronauts installed corrective optics that fixed Hubble's flawed vision.

missions.purpose: Space Radar Laboratory-1 (SRL-1) Earth imaging
Space Radar Laboratory-2 (SRL-2) Earth imaging
Astro-2 ultraviolet astronomy observatory
Wake Shield Facility-2 materials experiment
Retrieve Japan's Space Flyer Unit
SPACEHAB-4 research mission
Shuttle–Mir docking and crew exchange (the Shuttle–Mir program's 10th flight)
First International Space Station (ISS) assembly flight: the Unity node
missions.note: Joined Unity to the Russian-built Zarya module — the start of ISS assembly.

missions.purpose: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM)
missions.note: Mapped Earth's land surface in 3D with a 60 m radar mast.

missions.purpose: ISS assembly: P6 truss and solar arrays
ISS assembly: delivered Canadarm2
ISS Utilization Flight-1 and crew exchange
ISS Utilization Flight-2 and crew exchange
ISS assembly: P1 truss segment
missions.note: The last Shuttle flight before the Columbia accident.

missions.purpose: ISS assembly: S5 truss and equipment
missions.note: Barbara Morgan, the educator astronaut, flew aboard. The museum's payload bay is set up as for this mission.

missions.purpose: ISS assembly: first piece of Japan's Kibo lab and Canada's Dextre robot
ISS outfitting with the Leonardo logistics module; crew rotation
ISS assembly: completed Japan's Kibo lab (exposed facility)
ISS assembly: Tranquility (Node 3) and the Cupola observatory
ISS assembly: Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02); final flight
